analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to cover mental health and addiction like physical illness, enacted inside the $700 billion Wall Street bailout bill.
analysis.headline: The House passed a strong mental health parity bill 268-148 in March 2008, but the Senate never took it up; in October 2008 the parity language, weakened, was attached to the $700 billion Wall Street rescue bill, which passed the Senate 74-25 and the House 263-171 and was signed into law the same day.
analysis.plain_summary: This started as a bill requiring employer health plans to cover mental health and addiction treatment on the same terms as physical illness — same copays, same visit limits, no separate rules. The House passed it with wide support, but the Senate didn't take it up. Instead, when the financial system collapsed in the fall of 2008, Congress used this bill number as the vehicle for the $700 billion bank rescue, and the mental health parity language rode along as a tax-division rider — softer than the House version, with a cost-based exemption insurers could claim. President Bush signed it into law on October 3, 2008.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans with employer health insurance who have mental health or substance-use conditions gain equal coverage: the law bars plans from charging higher copays or setting tighter visit limits for mental health care than for physical care, and requires disclosure of denial criteria. Bank and financial institutions also gained the centerpiece of the enacted bill — a Treasury program authorized to purchase up to $700 billion of their troubled mortgage-backed assets. Homeowners and renters got foreclosure-mitigation and tenant-protection provisions, and renewable energy companies got extended and new tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients with mental health needs; banks

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans that cover mental health or addiction can no longer set higher deductibles, copays, or visit limits for that care than for medical or surgical care, and cannot impose separate treatment rules that apply only to mental health.
Plans must cover mental health and addiction care from out-of-network providers if they cover other care out-of-network, and must disclose the criteria used to deny mental health claims.

The House-passed version also extended parity to emergency care and required Labor Department audits of plan compliance, and would have increased the minimum Medicaid drug rebate to 20.1% — provisions that did not survive into the final law.

The enacted law also barred health plans and employers from using genetic information to deny coverage or employment, extended renewable energy and residential solar tax credits, and raised deposit insurance from $100,000 to $250,000.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the costs fall on employers and insurers who must equalize mental health benefits (some of which can be passed to premiums), on drug manufacturers under the House version's higher Medicaid rebate (dropped in the final law), and — most significantly in the final law — on taxpayers, who bore the risk of up to $700 billion in Treasury purchases of failing financial assets and a higher debt limit raised to $11.315 trillion.

drawbacks.text: The enacted parity rules let a plan escape the requirement for a full year if complying would raise total costs by more than 2% (then 1% in later years), a cost-based exit that gives insurers a route around the mandate.

The Senate version dropped provisions from the House-passed bill that would have raised the minimum Medicaid drug rebate paid by manufacturers from 15.1% to 20.1% and tightened rules on hospitals where physicians have financial interests, removing revenue offsets and self-dealing safeguards.

The rescue portion authorized up to $700 billion in Treasury purchases of banks' failing mortgage assets, with the decision largely delegated to the Treasury Secretary subject only to oversight boards and phased congressional disapproval.

The energy and tax portions extended a broad set of credits, including 30% investment tax credits for advanced coal and coal gasification projects with up to $2.55 billion in allocable credits, and extended credits for oil and gas production from marginal properties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mental health parity provisions deliver a real, lasting benefit: tens of millions of insured people got equal coverage for mental health and addiction treatment, a reform advocates had sought for over a decade. But the way it was enacted left a mixed record. The Senate version was weaker than the House-passed bill — it dropped the Medicaid drug-rebate increase, the tightened physician self-referral rules, and the Labor Department audit requirements, and gave insurers a first-year 2% cost escape hatch — and it rode to enactment inside the $700 billion bank rescue, a package the House had rejected days earlier and many members only accepted under crisis pressure. The good provision became law, but diluted, and the bill's central act was the largest financial-industry rescue in U.S. history.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed a strong parity bill in March 2008, but the Senate ignored it for seven months; in the October financial crisis, weakened parity language was folded into the $700 billion bank-rescue bill, which both chambers passed and the President signed on October 3, 2008.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in March 2007 to require group health plans to cover mental health and substance-use treatment on the same terms — same copays, deductibles, and visit limits — as medical and surgical care.
It drew 274 cosponsors in the House, including 41 Republicans, and cleared three House committees.

On the House floor in March 2008, Republicans offered motions to replace the bill with a weaker version; both failed, and the House passed the bill 268-148, with 221 of 231 Democrats voting yes and 47 of 198 Republicans.
The Senate received the House bill in March 2008 and placed it on its calendar, but did not act on it for seven months.

Instead, in October 2008 the Senate attached a weaker version of parity, named for Senator Pete Domenici, to the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act — the $700 billion bank rescue — along with energy tax credits and a package of expiring tax breaks.
That Senate package passed 74-25 on October 1, 2008, with 39 of 49 Democrats and 34 of 49 Republicans in favor.
The House agreed to the Senate version 263-171 on October 3, with 63 Democrats defecting, and President Bush signed it the same day as Public Law 110-343.

The enacted parity provisions cover the same core protections — equal cost-sharing and treatment limits, no separate mental health cost-sharing rules, disclosure of denial criteria — but dropped the House bill's Medicaid drug-rebate increase, hospital self-referral safeguards, and Labor Department audit mandate, and added a cost-based exemption letting plans escape the mandate for a year if compliance raises costs over 2%.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banking industry received the $700 billion rescue it needed in the crisis; health insurers kept their gatekeeper role with a new cost-based exemption. People with mental health and addiction coverage did win equal treatment, in weakened form.

sides.party_line_note: The March House vote split sharply by party — 221 of 231 Democrats for, 145 of 198 Republicans against — while the October votes were more bipartisan (34 of 49 Senate Republicans and 91 of 199 House Republicans for the final package), as the bank rescue reordered the coalitions.

industries.note: The enacted bill authorized Treasury to spend up to $700 billion buying their troubled mortgage-backed assets and to guarantee them, backstopping institutions whose losses helped trigger the crisis. It conditioned some aid on executive pay limits and profit-sharing warrants, but the central benefit — public money absorbing private losses — went to the financial sector.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: They must now cover mental health and addiction care on the same terms as physical care, which many had sharply limited. But they won a cost-based escape: if compliance raises costs more than 2% in year one or 1% after, an actuary can certify the plan exempt, and the final Senate version dropped the House's mandatory federal audits. Their gatekeeping role over care is regulated, not replaced.

The House-passed bill would have raised the minimum Medicaid drug rebate from 15.1% to 20.1%, forcing manufacturers to return more revenue on Medicaid prescriptions. That provision did not appear in the enacted Senate version, so the enacted law left their Medicaid pricing untouched while still delivering the parity mandate that brings more covered patients into treatment.

industries.industry: Renewable energy, solar, and wind industries
industries.note: The bill extended and expanded production and investment tax credits for wind, solar, geothermal, and efficiency, and created residential credits for rooftop solar and small wind. These credits lower energy costs and emissions over time, though they channel the subsidy through private projects and equipment makers.

The enacted package granted 30% investment tax credits for advanced coal and coal-gasification projects worth up to $2.55 billion, credits for carbon capture, and extended tax benefits for oil and gas production from marginal wells. These supports subsidize fossil fuel production at public expense.
